story.title: Meta makes the Muse filesystem even more accessible

facts.text: We asked Meta why Muse initially called filesystem access a security issue if it was always the intended behavior, and the company has not yet responded.
Yesterday, with a little prodding, it was discovered that Meta’s Muse would expose its filesystem to curious users.
Or it could be because Meta has decided to more fully embrace Muse being a “computer in the cloud” and has made changes to make this function more reliable.

In a statement provided to The Verge yesterday, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts said, “We’re continuing to make updates to the product, so users may see changes in how much information is available about their virtual machine.” And that seems to be the case.
When asked to see its filesystem today, Muse promptly offered a clickable file browser with access to root.
But today Muse will eagerly offer up the contents of its file system when you ask for it.
You can install software in it, write and compile code, use the browser to surf the web: it is your own Linux box that you can operate as you choose with your Muse.
Muse’s architecture is fundamentally different from other AI platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini.
A significant security concern has emerged surrounding Meta’s Muse after developers Peter James and Jonny L.

Both developers independently revealed that with minimal prompting, Muse was able to zip and provide access to its complete root filesystem, including Ubuntu system files, application templates, and internal documentation.
In response to the incident, Meta has confirmed that this behavior does not constitute a security breach.

Contradicting this, Nat Friedman from Meta Superintelligence Labs stated on Twitter that what was uncovered was “intended behavior.” This claim raises questions, especially since when the AI was first asked to share its filesystem, it declined, citing potential security risks.

Daniel Roberts, a spokesperson for Meta, asserted that Muse operates within persistent Linux virtual machines designed for individual users, emphasizing that exporting virtual machine data does not grant access to Meta’s underlying infrastructure or the data of other users.
Interesting findings highlighted by Saunders indicated that Muse could generate large amounts of accurate code swiftly, raising concerns about the implications of this capability.
Saunders, posting on Mastodon, described the process as “extremely easy” and noted Muse's lack of prompt injection resistance.

This incident marks the second security vulnerability associated with Muse that has come to light this week, following the discovery by security researcher Patrick Wardle, who revealed an exploit allowing potential hijacking of the AI agent and unauthorized access to a user's Muse account.
Meta responded quickly to this issue with a hotfix.

In an effort to replicate James and Saunders’ results, it was found that after starting a new session and prompting Muse appropriately, it produced “safe” versions of certain directories, significantly without sensitive items like SSH keys.
Additionally, mentions of a feature termed Meta Home Link were found, indicating possible hardware integration that would allow Muse to interact with devices on a home network.
Meta has yet to announce any such feature, leaving its future capability uncertain.
